title: A TCP/IP Tutorial
summary: A tutorial on the TCP/IP protocol suite, focused on the steps in forwarding an IP datagram from source host to destination host through a router. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1180 explains how data travels across a TCP/IP network. It shows the layers inside a computer, then follows a single packet from a sender, through a router, to the receiver.

questions: how is an ip datagram forwarded through a router
what is the tcp ip protocol stack
what is the difference between tcp and udp
subtitle: The layers and the routing of an IP datagram, explained step by step.

tldr.problem: People who worked with TCP/IP networks had descriptions of each protocol but few plain accounts of how the pieces fit together and how a packet actually travels.
tldr.mechanism: The tutorial draws the layered structure inside a computer, then follows one IP datagram from a sender to a router and on to the receiver, using the ARP table and the route table as the two tables that decide what happens.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that defines no standard; the authors state that its purpose is explanation, not definition, and that it updates and obsoletes no other RFC.

today: RFC 1180 is an Informational RFC that defines no standard, and it says so itself: the memo updates and obsoletes no other RFC. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. Its value is as a plain description of how the suite fits together, and it remains readable as a record of what the protocol suite looked like in January 1991.

sections.title: What the Tutorial Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1180 is a tutorial on the TCP/IP protocol suite, and it concentrates on the steps taken to forward an IP datagram from a source host to a destination host through a router. It says at the outset that it does not specify an Internet standard.

The authors are candid about the scope. They call it the bare bones of TCP/IP technology, and they list what it leaves out: the history of development and funding, the business case for using TCP/IP, and how it compares with ISO OSI. A great deal of technical information is omitted as well. What remains is the minimum a professional working in a TCP/IP environment needs, and the authors name that audience: systems administrators, systems programmers and network managers.

The examples come from the UNIX TCP/IP environment, but the memo says the main points apply across all implementations of TCP/IP. It closes the introduction with a warning that matters when the memo and a specification disagree: the purpose of the memo is explanation, not definition, so any question about the correct specification of a protocol should be referred to the actual standards.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a walk-through of how the TCP/IP protocols fit together, aimed at the people who run and program them. It covers only the essentials, and it says plainly that where it and a formal specification differ, the specification wins.

sections.title: The Layers Inside a Computer
sections.content:
The tutorial starts from a diagram of the logical structure inside a computer. At the top sit the network applications. Below them sit TCP and UDP, side by side. Below them is IP, with ARP off to one side, and at the bottom the Ethernet driver and the Ethernet cable. The boxes represent the processing the data goes through; the lines show its path. A running computer always knows its own IP address and its own Ethernet address.

The IP module sits at the centre. Each module or driver adds a header as a message travels down the stack and strips that header off as the message travels back up. The IP header carries the IP address, and that is what turns several physical networks into a single logical network, which is where the word internet comes from. A set of interconnected physical networks that limit the range of an IP packet is called an internet.

IP also hides the hardware from applications. A new physical network can be put into service by writing a new driver to sit underneath IP, and the applications above do not have to change. The memo also names the property that makes this work across suppliers: two computers that can communicate are said to interoperate.

A computer with more than one network interface has a separate Ethernet address and a separate IP address for each of them, and its IP module becomes a multiplexer in both directions. Sending an IP packet out onto another network is called forwarding, and a computer dedicated to that task is called an IP-router. A forwarded packet never reaches the TCP or UDP modules on the router, and some routers have no TCP or UDP module at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer is built as a stack of layers: applications on top, then TCP or UDP, then IP, then the network hardware. Each layer adds its own header as data goes down and removes it as data comes back up. IP is the layer that ties separate networks into one logical network.

sections.title: How ARP Finds the Ethernet Address
sections.content:
Before an IP packet can go out on Ethernet, the sender needs the destination's Ethernet address. ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, supplies it. The translation is done only for outgoing packets, because that is when the IP header and the Ethernet header are created.

The translation comes from a table in memory with one row per computer and two columns: an IP address and an Ethernet address. The table exists because no algorithm can derive one address from the other. The IP address is chosen by the network manager according to where the computer sits on the internet, and it changes when the computer moves. The Ethernet address is chosen by the manufacturer and changes when the hardware is replaced.

When the table has no entry, two things happen. The host sends an ARP request with a broadcast Ethernet address, so every computer on the network receives it, and it queues the IP packet it was trying to send. The request carries the sender's IP and Ethernet addresses and the target IP address, and asks: if this is your IP address, please tell me your Ethernet address. The machine that owns the target address replies directly to the sender with the sender and target fields swapped. The sender's ARP module then adds the new pair to its table, and the queued packet goes out with the address filled in. The memo notes that the translation arrives just milli-seconds after it was needed.

Two failure cases are described. Each computer keeps a separate ARP table per Ethernet interface. If the target computer does not exist there is no response and no table entry, so IP discards outgoing packets to that address, and the upper layer protocols cannot tell the difference between a broken Ethernet and a missing computer. Some implementations do not queue the packet at all: they discard it and leave recovery to the TCP module or the UDP application, which uses time-out and retransmission.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer cannot work out a hardware address from an IP address, so it asks. It broadcasts a request asking who owns that IP address, queues the packet it wanted to send, and sends it on as soon as the answer arrives.

sections.title: How IP Decides Where to Send a Packet
sections.content:
The memo says the essence of IP is its route table, an in-memory table whose contents are set by the network administrator, and that mistakes in it block communication. For an outgoing packet, IP consults the route table to decide whether to deliver the packet directly or indirectly and which lower interface to use. For an incoming packet, IP decides whether to forward it or pass it up; a forwarded packet is treated as an outgoing one, and is never sent back out through the interface it arrived on.

Direct routing is the simple case. When A sends to B on the same network, the IP header carries A's source address and B's destination address, and the Ethernet header carries A's and B's Ethernet addresses. In the tutorial's larger example, three IP networks are joined by a router that has three IP addresses, three Ethernet addresses and only one IP module. When A sends to a host on another network, the IP header still says A and the final destination, but the Ethernet header names the router, because that is the next hop.

The route table has one row per route. Its columns are the IP network number, a direct or indirect flag, the router's IP address and the interface number. On most computers it is changed with the route command and displayed by netstat -r. IP extracts the network part of the destination address and scans the first column for a match; a miss means the packet is discarded, and some computers report a network not reachable error.

IP addresses are 4 bytes, split by the network manager into a network number and a host number: 223.1.2.1 is network 223.1.2 and host 1. The tutorial's example addresses are class C, where the upper three bits mark 21 bits of network number and 8 bits of host number, allowing 2,097,152 networks of up to 254 hosts. The IP address space is administered by the Network Information Center.

Names live in two plain files. The hosts file maps an IP address to a computer name, and the networks file maps a network number to a network name. These files are not needed to run an internet, but they make it easier to work with. A long path is not worked out centrally: each router consults its own table and contributes only the next hop, and the whole route is the result of those local decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: IP decides where a packet goes by looking up the destination in a table of routes. If the destination is on a directly connected network, the packet goes straight out. Otherwise the table names a router to hand it to, and the packet keeps the final destination address all the way.

sections.title: Two Ways to Move Data: UDP and TCP
sections.content:
UDP and TCP both sit on top of IP and supply different services, and the memo's answer to why both exist is that applications need different things. UDP is a connectionless datagram delivery service that does not guarantee delivery; it keeps no end-to-end connection and simply pushes datagrams out and accepts them in. It adds two things to IP: the multiplexing of applications by port number, and a checksum that checks the integrity of the data.

Ports are numbered starting at zero. A server waits on the port dedicated to its service, so the SNMP agent always waits on port 161 and only one can exist per computer, and the TELNET server uses port 23 of TCP. UDP preserves the boundaries the application set: five writes produce five reads of the same size, and a message is never joined to another or split apart.

On checksums, the memo notes that a checksum of zero means the sender did not calculate one and can be ignored, so a sending computer may or may not compute it. If Ethernet is the only network between the two ends, checksumming may not be needed, but it is recommended to keep it enabled, because a later change to the route table may send the data across less reliable media. If the checksum is valid or zero and an application is bound to the destination port, the message is queued for that application; otherwise the datagram is discarded. If datagrams arrive faster than the application can read them and the queue fills, UDP discards them until there is room.

TCP offers a connection-oriented byte stream and guarantees delivery. It is used by applications that need guaranteed delivery and would rather not handle time-outs and retransmissions themselves, such as FTP and TELNET, and also by X-Window and the remote command family. The cost is more CPU and network bandwidth, and the TCP module is much more complicated than the UDP module. The two ends hold state that defines a virtual circuit, and data can travel in both directions at once.

TCP packetises the byte stream at will and keeps no record of the boundaries between writes: five writes might arrive as ten reads, or as one. It is a sliding window protocol with time-out and retransmission, outgoing data must be acknowledged, and acknowledgements can be piggybacked on data. Both ends can flow control the far end, which prevents a buffer overrun. The window size fixes how much data may be sent before an acknowledgement is required, and for TCP that amount is a number of bytes rather than a number of segments.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP sends single messages and does not check that they arrive. TCP joins everything into one continuous stream of bytes and makes sure it arrives. Applications that need every message delivered in order choose TCP; applications that want speed and can handle loss choose UDP.

sections.title: Applications, Security and Further Reading
sections.content:
The tutorial ends by naming the applications it has discussed and by pointing onward. TELNET gives remote login over TCP, as if dialling a telephone switchboard, and has widespread interoperability between different operating systems. FTP, as old as TELNET, also uses TCP and copies files. The remote command family for UNIX, with commands such as rcp, rwho, rsh and rlogin, works between trusted hosts and, as the memo puts it, little consideration is given to security. NFS, developed by Sun Microsystems, uses UDP to mount UNIX file systems, although it adds significant load to a network and is of poor use across slow links. SNMP uses UDP so that central stations can collect data, defining the format of the data but leaving the interpretation to the manager. The X Window System draws windows over TCP.

For anyone who wants to go further, the memo lists the next level of detail: the administration commands arp, route and netstat; permanent, publish and time-out entries in the ARP table and the subject of ARP spoofing; host entries, a default gateway and subnets in the IP route table; the time-to-live counter, fragmentation and ICMP; RIP and routing loops; and the Domain Name System.

The Security Considerations section is candid. It says there are security considerations within the TCP/IP protocol suite, that for some people they are serious problems and for others they are not depending on user requirements, and that the tutorial does not discuss them. It points the reader to start with ARP spoofing and then use the Security Considerations section of RFC 1122 to go further.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo closes with the applications it covered, a list of topics to read next, and a short note on security. It does not claim the protocol suite is free of security problems; it says the subject is out of scope and points to RFC 1122.
